title: ART urges further reforms as gender super gap persists
full_text:
Australian Retirement Trust (ART) has warned that Australia’s gender pay gap continues to translate into significantly lower retirement savings for women, despite growing evidence they are taking a more active role in managing their superannuation.
Marking Equal Pay Day on 17 August, the nation’s second-largest super fund said the annual milestone highlighted more than differences in wages, arguing the impact of lower earnings compounds throughout a person’s working life and into retirement.
The Workplace Gender Equality Agency has designated 17 August as Equal Pay Day this year, reflecting the additional 48 days women must work to earn what men earned on average in the previous financial year.
As it stands today, Australia’s national gender pay gap is 11.3 per cent.
According to the fund, Australian women typically retire with around $50,000 less superannuation than men, while its Financial Wellbeing Index found 62 per cent of women feared they would not have enough money for retirement, compared with 49 per cent of men.
New member data released by the fund showed women were more likely than men to make voluntary super contributions during the 2025–26 financial year, with 17.7 per cent of female members contributing extra to their accounts compared with 10.4 per cent of male members.
Women were also more likely to benefit from financial advice, with that rate increasing slightly over the year.
“It’s encouraging to see women taking action where they can,” said Anne Fuchs, executive general manager, advocacy and impact, at Australian Retirement Trust.
“But women shouldn’t have to solve the gender super gap on their own. Closing it needs policy reform, action from employers and practical support over time.”
ART found that lower wages, career breaks, part-time employment and unpaid caring responsibilities all contribute to smaller retirement balances over time.
Research cited by the fund stated that women aged between 60 and 64 held median super balances around 25 per cent lower than men, while ART’s own member analysis showed women approaching retirement at age 60 had around 23 per cent less super than their male counterparts.
“Lower pay, career breaks, part-time work and unpaid caring responsibilities can all reduce super over time,” Fuchs said. “So the gender pay gap becomes a gender super gap.”
The fund noted that two reforms it had advocated for had now become law, including the introduction of superannuation on government-funded parental leave and an increase to the Low Income Super Tax Offset from July 2027 aimed at improving retirement outcomes for low-income earners.
ART said further changes were still needed, including extending super to people receiving the Carer Payment, removing the 30-hour eligibility rule for many workers under 18, and recognising unpaid care work more effectively.
“The gender super gap exists because of decades of structural inequality,” Fuchs said. “Closing it means fixing the system, while giving women the tools to take control of their super. Small moves really can make a difference, but the system has to move too.”
Alongside broader policy reforms, ART encouraged women concerned about their retirement savings to review their super balance, understand their investment options, consider making additional contributions where possible and seek guidance or financial advice.
“A place to start is investing in your own financial literacy, making the most of the education your super fund offers, or getting personal financial advice,” Fuchs said. “The best time to start is today.”
